analysis.one_liner: Caps donations to Super PACs at the same limit as regular political committees.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap Super PAC contributions was introduced with 33 Democratic cosponsors, sent to the House Administration Committee, and has had no hearing or vote since March 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Abolish Super PACs Act would change federal campaign finance law so that committees that make independent political expenditures — Super PACs — are subject to the same per-person contribution limits as ordinary political committees, instead of the unlimited amounts they can take now. A single donor would be limited to the standard cap per year rather than tens or hundreds of millions. The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee, where it has sat without action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters gain a campaign finance system where candidates cannot rely on unlimited checks from a handful of mega-donors. The bill's findings note that the top 1 percent of individual Super PAC contributors supplied 96.94 percent of all individual Super PAC contributions in 2024, so capping contributions would shift influence back toward small donors and voters [S2]. Candidates without access to a single $100-million contributor would face a less lopsided playing field. The bill also argues the caps would make it harder for foreign money to flow into Super PACs through middlemen [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'independent expenditure committees' to the categories of political committees subject to federal contribution limits, so donations to a Super PAC would be capped at the same per-donor limit that already applies to other political committees, rather than unlimited.

The bill's findings argue that unlimited Super PAC money creates a real corruption risk, because large contributors can route money through a Super PAC to influence a candidate, and that a bipartisan majority of Americans believe large Super PAC contributions are made in exchange for political favors.

It would shrink the concentration of campaign money in a few hands: the bill cites that the top 1 percent of individual Super PAC contributors gave 76.76 percent of individual Super PAC contributions in 2012, rising to 96.94 percent in 2024, with recent elections influenced by individual contributors who gave more than $100 million.
It would also make it harder for foreign entities to funnel money into U.S. elections through third-party contributors into Super PACs, according to the bill's findings.

analysis.who_pays: Ultra-wealthy donors and Super PACs would bear the cost. Donors who now can give unlimited amounts — the bill notes some individuals gave more than $100 million to Super PACs — would be limited to the standard political committee cap. Super PACs themselves, about 2,459 of which were registered as of the 2024 cycle, and the political fundraising and consulting economy built around their spending (over $4.48 billion in independent expenditures in 2024) would see their funding streams shrink. Candidates in both parties would lose access to the Super PAC funding channel that the bill says has become critical to winning federal campaigns.

drawbacks.text: The contribution limits would likely face a serious court challenge. A federal appeals court (SpeechNow.org v. FEC, D.C. Circuit, 2010) previously voided contribution limits on independent-expenditure groups, and this bill would directly reinstate them; the bill's own findings acknowledge and dispute that ruling, but a court could block the caps from taking effect.

The bill caps contributions to Super PACs but does not cap independent spending itself, so wealthy donors could shift money to other vehicles — such as nonprofit groups that do not disclose donors — rather than the money leaving politics entirely.

Candidates and party committees in both parties would lose a major funding channel; the bill's findings say obtaining millions or billions in Super PAC money is now critical to the success of federal candidates' campaigns, so the change would disrupt how campaigns are financed with no transition period beyond the first calendar year after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a campaign finance system less dominated by a tiny group of ultra-wealthy donors, with a lower risk of corruption or the appearance of it. The costs are real but mostly fall on concentrated interests: mega-donors, Super PACs, and the fundraising industry around them. The design is simple — it reuses existing contribution limits rather than inventing new ones — but it leaves independent spending itself unlimited and would likely be tested in court immediately, so its practical effect is uncertain even if it passed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Administration Committee, which has not scheduled a hearing or a vote on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Summer Lee of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on March 26, 2025, joined by six original cosponsors: Reps. Khanna, McGovern, Jayapal, Tlaib, Deluzio, and Ramirez.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, which holds jurisdiction over campaign finance and election law.
The bill has attracted 33 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats; no Republican has signed on.
Since the referral, the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — leaving the bill sitting in committee as the two-year Congress continues.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nobody has won anything from this bill — the bigger beneficiaries of the status quo are Super PACs and their large donors, who continue to give unlimited amounts while the bill waits in committee.

for.name: Rep. Summer Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Abolish Super PACs Act and recruited six original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 33 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Khanna, McGovern, Jayapal, Tlaib, Deluzio, and Ramirez.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration (chair Rep. Bryan Steil, R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 26, 2025 and has taken no further action on it — no hearing or markup has been scheduled in the record.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsors have signed on, and with a Republican majority, a bill with none is unlikely to be scheduled for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: Super PACs exist to accept unlimited contributions and spend them on elections; the bill would cap their donations at the same per-donor limit as ordinary committees, eliminating their defining advantage. 2,459 Super PACs were registered and spent a combined $4.48 billion in independent expenditures in 2024.

The top 1 percent of individual contributors supplied 96.94 percent of all individual Super PAC contributions in 2024, and some gave more than $100 million; the caps would end their ability to buy outsized influence through this channel.
Firms that raise and deploy Super PAC money — over $4.48 billion in independent expenditures in 2024 — would see the pool of money they manage shrink to contribution-capped levels.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to committee never get a hearing, and this one has shown no movement in months. With 33 cosponsors from only one party, no Republican support, and a Republican-controlled House Administration Committee, the bill is very likely to sit in committee until the Congress ends on January 3, 2027 without a vote.
